Workflows, assistants and agents: choosing the shape

Three shapes, one question

Learning objective — Tell a fixed workflow, an assistant and an agent apart.

Core principle

The difference is who decides the next step: your code, a person, or the model at run time.

Evidence from the field

Anthropic’s guide Building effective agents (December 2024) defines workflows as systems where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, and agents as systems where the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use. The iSAQB AGENTA curriculum (2026.1-rev5, learning goal 1-4) asks learners to distinguish assistants from agents and to explain the agentic loop.

Engineering response

For each task, write down who chooses the next step, then name the shape.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

A script calls a model to summarise every email and files it in a fixed folder. Is that a workflow, an assistant or an agent?

Workflows, assistants and agents: choosing the shape

Start with the simplest thing that works

Learning objective — Justify the simplest shape that meets the need.

Core principle

Every step of autonomy adds cost, delay and new ways to fail, so make each step earn its place.

Evidence from the field

The same guide advises finding the simplest solution possible and adding complexity only when it clearly improves results, because agentic systems trade speed and cost for performance. AGENTA learning goal 1-2 includes knowing when to use people, classic tools or agents.

Engineering response

Ask in order: can plain code do it, can a fixed workflow of model calls do it, and only then, can it be an agent?

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Name one task in your own work where plain code beats a model.

Workflows, assistants and agents: choosing the shape

Four signals that call for an agent

Learning objective — Score a task against signals for run-time decision making.

Core principle

An agent earns its place when the path cannot be written in advance, the result can be checked against something real, a wrong step is cheap to undo, and the cost per run is acceptable.

Evidence from the field

These four signals are Intellica’s working checklist, not a published standard. A coding task whose result is checked by a test suite scores well on all four; an open-ended request to “make customers happier” scores badly on the second.

Engineering response

Score the task on each signal as yes, partly or no before you pick a shape, and write the reason.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

Why is “the tests pass” a good signal for an agent and “the reader will like it” a poor one?

Workflows, assistants and agents: choosing the shape

Record the decision

Learning objective — Write the shape as a reviewable architectural decision.

Core principle

The shape is an architectural decision: it has reasons, rejected options and a trigger for revisiting it.

Evidence from the field

AGENTA section 2 treats architectural decisions as hypotheses to test. The iSAQB Foundation curriculum release candidate 2027.1-RC1 (valid from 1 April 2027, still a preview) adds learning goal 05-01: decide, against stated criteria, whether and how to use AI for a task, and justify that as an architectural decision.

Engineering response

Use a five-line record: task, options considered, choice, reasons, and the event that would make you revisit it.

RETRIEVAL & DESIGN CHECK

What event would make you move a workflow to an agent, or an agent back to a workflow?

titles: Start with the simplest thing that works
Four signals that call for an agent

quiz.q: What mainly separates a workflow from an agent?
o: The workflow uses a smaller model.
In a workflow your code fixes the path; in an agent the model chooses its steps at run time.
quiz.why: The difference is who decides the next step. A workflow can call a model, but the code sets the path.

quiz.q: Which task most favours an agent?
o: Convert each invoice to a PDF with a fixed template.
Fix a failing build where a test suite can confirm each attempt and a wrong change is easy to revert.
Send the same reminder every Monday.
quiz.why: The path is not known in advance, the result is checkable and mistakes are cheap to undo.

quiz.q: Why record the shape decision with a revisit trigger?
o: It is required by every standard.
So a later incident or cost surprise shows which assumption failed.
Because agents cannot be changed afterwards.
quiz.why: A trigger turns the choice into a testable hypothesis, as AGENTA section 2 recommends.

ps: Most teams meet agents through a demo, and the demo skips the question this lesson asks: should this part of the system decide anything at run time at all? A fixed workflow is easier to test, cheaper to run and simpler to explain to an auditor. An assistant keeps a person in charge of every step. An agent chooses its own steps, which is powerful when the path is unknowable and risky when it is not. Treat the three as a ladder and climb only as far as the task forces you.

The four signals are a conversation starter. Score honestly, write the reason next to each score, and keep the record. When a later incident or a cost surprise happens, the record tells you which assumption failed. That is what turns the choice from a mood into an engineering decision.

Illustrative case. Doubles-to-Go lets street-food vendors take orders in an app. Customers complain about missing items and late orders, and vendors want help answering. The team lists three designs. A: a fixed workflow that classifies each complaint with a model and routes it to a template reply. B: an assistant that drafts replies for the vendor to approve. C: an agent that reads the order, checks the payment, decides on a refund and writes to the customer. They score the task: the path varies (partly), the result can be checked against the order record (yes), a wrong refund is not cheap to undo (no), cost per case matters (partly). They choose B for the first release and write the trigger: move refunds under TT$50 to an agent only after sixty days of vendor-approved drafts show a correct-decision rate they have agreed in advance.
Mark your own work against these four criteria. Score each 0, 1 or 2.
